theme: The rich; patience; prayer; restoring the wanderer
readingInstruction: Read James 5:1-20. James closes with a warning to the rich, a call to patience, and instruction on prayer and care for one another. Notice how often James points to the coming of the Lord.
settingTheScene: Many of the first Christians were poor, and landowners sometimes withheld wages from day laborers. James speaks like an Old Testament prophet against such injustice. He then turns to the suffering believers and calls them to wait for the Lord’s return with patience, like a farmer waiting for rain. The letter ends with a practical section on prayer, anointing the sick, and restoring those who wander.
observation: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you” (v. 1).
“Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord” (v. 7).
“Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast” (v. 11).
“Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray” (v. 13).
“Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord” (v. 14).
“The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working” (v. 16).
“Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain” (v. 17).
“Whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins” (v. 20).
interpretation:
James speaks to the wealthy who trust in riches: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten. Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you.” Their sin is hoarding in the last days, and especially withholding the wages of the laborers who mowed their fields. Those cries have “reached the ears of the Lord of hosts.” They have lived in luxury and self-indulgence, fattening their hearts “in a day of slaughter,” and have condemned and murdered the righteous person, who does not resist. James is not condemning wealth in itself but its misuse and the injustice by which it was gained.

Then he turns to the suffering: “Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord.” The farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient until it receives the early and the late rains. “You also, be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.” Do not grumble against one another. The Judge is standing at the door. For examples, he points to the prophets and to Job: “You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.” Our suffering has a purpose, and the Lord’s character is compassion. He also warns against oaths: “Let your yes be yes and your no be no.” Be people whose word is reliable.

The final section is about prayer. “Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.” The church should pray in every circumstance. “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.” Christians differ on the meaning of the anointing: some take it as medicinal (oil was used as medicine), some as symbolic of setting apart for God, and some as a sacramental act. In every reading, the healing comes from the Lord, not the oil, and the emphasis is on prayer by the elders. Not every sick person is healed in this life, as Paul’s thorn and Timothy’s ailments show, but the Lord hears and may raise up.

“Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.” Elijah is the example. He “was a man with a nature like ours,” yet when he prayed, the rain stopped for three and a half years, and when he prayed again, the heavens gave rain. We are as weak as Elijah, but we pray to the same God. The letter ends without a benediction, with a charge: if anyone wanders from the truth and someone brings him back, “let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.” Caring for a wandering brother is among the most loving things a Christian can do.
connection: Deuteronomy 24:14-15 and Leviticus 19:13 forbid withholding wages. Isaiah 5:8-10 and Amos 5:11-12 are prophetic warnings against the rich. Matthew 6:19-21 and Luke 12:16-21 speak of treasure. Deuteronomy 11:14 mentions early and late rains. Job 42:10-17 shows the end of Job’s story. Matthew 5:33-37 is Jesus’ teaching on oaths. Mark 6:13 mentions anointing the sick. 1 Kings 17-18 is the Elijah account. Galatians 6:1 and Matthew 18:15 speak of restoring a brother. Proverbs 10:12 and 1 Peter 4:8 say love covers a multitude of sins.
application:
Be honest about how you use money. Ask whether you are being generous or hoarding, and whether you pay what you owe.

Pray for someone who is sick, and ask your pastor how your church cares for the sick.

Think of someone who has wandered from the faith. Pray for them, and reach out this week with love.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from trusting in riches or using them unjustly.
Ask him to give you patience.
Pray for someone who has wandered, and ask what you might do.
